newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Amid U.S. concerns, Havel warns Czechs on defence.
newsitem.headline: Amid U.S. concerns, Havel warns Czechs on defence.

text.p: Czech President Vaclav Havel, a strong advocate of NATO membership, warned the nation on Monday against regarding military spending as a luxury, saying Czechs must accept their role in a common defence of democracy.

Havel made his comments in a National Day speech following U.S. expressions of concern that the Czech Republic may not be spending enough on defence for a country determined to be one of the first former East Bloc states to join NATO.
"No concrete and visible enemy is threatening our republic today. Therefore many people think that defence spending is a luxury, if not a direct waste of money," he said.
U.S. President Bill Clinton called last week for the Western alliance to recruit its first post-communist members by 1999.
Havel indicated that the Czech Republic had to back up its claim to be among the frontrunners when NATO decides next year on which countries should join.

"Now, when for the first time in our history we have the chance to incorporate our country firmly into the wider ties of the defence of the democratic world, we have to show that we intend to participate seriously in this defence," he said.

Czech diplomats say U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher and United Nations ambassador Madeleine Albright have expressed concern about what they regard as the low level of Czech defence spending.
The worries were expressed during meetings with Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus and Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec.

Klaus denied last week that Christopher had said this when they met in September. But in an indication of differences within the ruling Civic Democratic Party, the Foreign Ministry confirmed that the subject had been raised.

"Right now when new political and security organisations are being born for the European continent and the whole world, the time is coming when we have to show clearly that we want to bear our portion of responsibility for peace and the general defence of human dignitity and all values which secure it," said Havel.
In the 1997 budget, which faces two more parliamentary readings, defence spending at 32 billion crowns ($1.2 billion) is only 4.8 percent higher than the original 1996 budget.

But the government recently cut 1996 spending across the board due to lower than expected revenue. This makes proposed 1997 defence spending 8.5 percent above the revised level, in line with inflation but well short of the 18.4 percent increase in the overall budget.

Czechs have found themselves in a security vacuum since the 1989 fall of communism. Prague is determined to join NATO to avoid a repeat of disasters in history, notably in 1938 when Britain and France authorised Nazi Germany to annex large parts of the former Czechoslovakia.

"Modern European history shows us sufficiently that the best path to war and human suffering is when democracies underestimate their own defence in peacetime or when they do not have enough courage ... when it is needed," said Havel.
